title: Delta Air Lines Atlanta Data Center Power Failure Grounds the Global Fleet
dcName: Delta Technology Data Center, Atlanta Headquarters

severity.usersAffected: Tens of thousands of passengers worldwide; thousands stranded overnight and sleeping on airport floors (exact passenger count not stated by any source)
severity.tier: Critical (SEV-1 equivalent; full worldwide operational outage)

brief: In the early hours of 8 August 2016, a routine scheduled transfer of load onto a backup generator at Delta Air Lines' Atlanta headquarters data center precipitated a fire in the power control room. The fire failed a transformer and cut a primary power path feeding the facility. Roughly 300 of Delta's 7,000 servers lacked a working alternate feed and went dark, and because surviving servers could no longer communicate with the failed nodes, the entire airline operations platform collapsed. Delta grounded its global fleet, cancelling about 2,100 flights over three days and delaying another 2,400, at an estimated cost of ~$150 million. CEO Ed Bastian took full responsibility. The event is a textbook case of a common-mode power fault upstream of server-level redundancy defeating an otherwise diverse design, compounded by a tightly-coupled system with no graceful degradation and an unmodernized legacy reservation tier.

magnitude.note: Financial impact (~$150M) is roughly 200x the Ponemon industry-average data-center outage cost (~$730K per the cited source), hence a 9. Blast radius is near-total: a ~4% node loss (300 of 7,000 servers) cascaded into a 100% platform outage that grounded a global fleet across 334 destinations in 64 countries. Core power/IT restoration took ~6 hours (durationScore 7 reflects this rather than the 3-day operational tail). Users score reflects tens of thousands stranded worldwide, though no exact passenger figure was published.

sequenceOfEvents.event: A routine scheduled switch for testing purposes transferred load onto the backup generator. This control action precipitated a fire in the power control room of Delta's Atlanta data center.

The fire caused a transformer to fail, killing one of the two power feeds serving the data center. The primary source and the switching-in backup generator both sat at the local power-control-room equipment that burned; the geographically separate second utility feed on the opposite side of the building survived.

300 of Delta's 7,000 servers were not linked to an alternate power source. Servers powered only by the failed feed went down; many could not fail over because their designated backups were also unpowered.

Surviving and dual-fed servers stayed powered but could no longer communicate with the failed nodes. In the tightly-coupled distributed system, loss of the subset broke shared state and hard dependencies, taking down Delta's entire platform: check-in, baggage, websites, kiosks, airport displays, scheduling and fueling.

Georgia Power dispatched workers for a switch-gear problem but reported no outages in its own territory and that other customers were unaffected, confirming the fault was internal to Delta's switchgear/transformer rather than a grid outage.
Recovery required rebooting 500 servers to bring the platform back online.

Delta systems were operational again about six hours after the fire. On recovery, only the old Deltamatic green-screen interface worked, forcing most agents to check in passengers manually and hand-write boarding passes.
The FAA ground stop on Delta was lifted, but cancellations and delays continued as the operation recovered.
By 1:30 PM only 1,700 of Delta's ~6,000 scheduled flights were operating; a midday tally recorded 451 flights cancelled and 1,679 operated so far.
Delta cancelled about 2,100 flights over three days (1,000 Monday, 800 Tuesday, 300 Wednesday) and delayed a further 2,400. Thousands of passengers slept on airport floors awaiting flights.

rootCause:
TRIGGER. In the early morning of 8 August 2016, an electric problem at Delta Air Lines' Atlanta headquarters ('technology command center') caused a power loss. Per the Wall Street Journal, the fault 'occurred at 2:30 a.m. ET.' Georgia Power — the Southern Co.-owned utility that serves nearly the entire state — said its technicians responded and concluded the issue was a failed 'switchgear' (the WSJ likened switchgear to 'a fuse box at home that routes the power in and distributes it throughout the house'). Delta CEO Ed Bastian characterized the initiating element more specifically as 'a power control module at the airline's technology command center [that] failed and caught fire,' while Georgia Power 'said the outage was caused by the failure of Delta switchgear equipment, which switches power flows within a system.' Both first parties therefore located the failed component in Delta-side electrical distribution equipment, not on Georgia Power's grid; Georgia Power stated: 'We believe that Delta Air Lines experienced an equipment failure overnight that caused their outage.'

LOSS OF POWER AND RESERVE. Per the ASA Institute for Risk & Innovation risk note, 'On August 8th 2016, Delta lost access to Georgia Powers and its reserve generator, due to a power outage,' producing a 'shutdown of Delta's data center, which controls bookings, flight operations and other critical systems.' The failure thus removed both the utility feed and Delta's on-site backup generation. One reported (speculative) mechanism — Reuters reporting quoted by WSWS — is that Delta 'was probably running a routine test of its backup power supplies when the switchgear failed and locked Delta out of its reserve generators.' This is hedged as 'probably' and is reported speculation, not a confirmed finding.

REDUNDANCY / FAILOVER FAILURE (the decisive IT failure). The most consequential failure was the incomplete automatic failover of the IT estate. In Delta's own words, reported by the WSJ, 'some critical systems and network equipment didn't switch over to Delta's backup systems,' while (per Delta's operations update, quoted by the ASA note) 'Other systems did.' Because a subset of critical booking and flight-operations systems and network equipment did not transfer, the data center that runs check-in, departure control and displays went dark, and those systems remained down even after power was restored, requiring manual recovery. Delta said 'it is investigating the cause.'

ESCALATION. With the data center down, Delta held hundreds of departing aircraft on the ground beginning at 5 a.m. ET, producing a global ground stop. Flights resumed 'taking off at about 9 a.m. ET,' but because systems recovered unevenly, cancellations cascaded: Delta 'canceled more than 650 flights, or about 10% of its daily total on Monday' and 'operated 2,340 flights of about 6,000 scheduled to fly.' Per the ASA note (citing Fortune), Delta 'cancelled 2,300 flights over three days and its revenue for August 2016 declined approximately $100 million.'

UNDERLYING VULNERABILITY. The WSJ situated the failure within Delta's aging, merged IT estate — systems 'that date from the 1990s,' with Delta having 'merged with Northwest Airlines eight years ago' — which made failover behavior harder to guarantee under a real power loss. It must be stated plainly: there is NO official, regulatory, court, or vendor engineering post-incident review of this event. The authoritative record consists of first-party statements (Delta and Georgia Power) reported through the press, plus a secondary private risk analysis (ASA). The deeper question of exactly why specific critical systems failed to fail over was left, per Delta, 'under investigation' and was not publicly resolved in the available sources.
contributingFactors: Incomplete/partial automatic failover (decisive): Delta's own statement, reported by the WSJ, is that 'some critical systems and network equipment didn't switch over to Delta's backup systems'; the ASA note adds Delta's line that 'Other systems did.' A redundancy architecture that transfers only part of the critical estate under a real power loss converted a single equipment failure into a total operational outage. Delta said it was 'investigating the cause.'

Single point of failure in the power distribution path: A single failed switchgear (a 'power control module,' per CEO Bastian) at the Atlanta technology command center removed the power feed, and per the ASA note simultaneously cost Delta 'access to Georgia Powers and its reserve generator' — indicating insufficient electrical redundancy/isolation so that one component's failure cascaded to the whole data center.

Loss of backup generation coincident with the fault: Per the ASA note Delta 'lost access to Georgia Powers and its reserve generator.' Reuters reporting (quoted by WSWS) offers one hedged, unconfirmed explanation — that a routine test of the backup power supplies was in progress and the switchgear failure 'locked Delta out of its reserve generators.' If accurate, a maintenance/test procedure able to strand the reserve during a fault is an organizational/procedural contributor; note this mechanism is reported as 'probably,' not confirmed.

Aging and merged IT systems: The WSJ attributes underlying fragility to systems 'that date from the 1990s' and to the still-imperfect integration after Delta 'merged with Northwest Airlines eight years ago,' leaving a heterogeneous estate whose failover behavior was not uniformly reliable.

Concentration/criticality of the affected data center: The single Atlanta data center 'controls bookings, flight operations and other critical systems' (ASA, quoting Delta/Reuters), so its loss immediately grounded the global fleet — a concentration-of-function risk with insufficient independent operating capability during the outage.

coe.action: Implement immediate, reliable, automatic failover at every layer (server, data store, network component) so any single-component loss is absorbed transparently rather than cascading. NOTE: this is the source analyst's prescriptive remediation principle, not an announced Delta corrective action.
coe.status: Recommended (source prescription; no official Delta action plan published)

coe.action: Re-map and remediate the 300 single-corded servers so every server's redundant power supplies are genuinely fed from independent, separately-powered strips/feeds. INFERRED corrective from the identified latent defect; not a verified announced action.
coe.status: Gap — no verified source confirms this was performed

coe.action: Introduce fault-domain diversity at the power transfer/control node (independent switchgear/transformer paths) so a localized power-room fire cannot take out both the primary source and the switching-in backup simultaneously. INFERRED from the common-mode analysis; not a verified announced action.
coe.status: Gap — no verified equipment-level RCA or remediation published

coe.action: Modernize or retire the Deltamatic legacy reservation tier and ensure recovery/fallback paths are themselves designed to degrade gracefully rather than collapsing to a green-screen-only mode. INFERRED from the recovery outcome; not a verified announced action.
coe.status: Gap — not confirmed by any verified source

coe.action: CEO accepted accountability publicly — Ed Bastian took full responsibility for the failure, and Delta issued refunds, $200 vouchers, waived change fees, hoteled thousands of passengers, and used its private-jet fleet for top-tier customers.
coe.status: Done (customer remediation executed during the event)

lessonsLearnt: Geographic path diversity is not fault-domain diversity: two feeds entering opposite sides of a building buy nothing once both converge at a shared transfer/control node, which becomes a single common-mode point of failure.
Redundancy that is not verified is not redundancy: 300 servers were 'supposed to be' dual-corded but were not, and the gap was invisible until a real power loss made it matter.

Planned maintenance and redundancy tests are among the most dangerous moments in a data center; taking the normal source out of the path to prove the backup can trigger the exact outage the test is meant to prevent.
Tight coupling without graceful degradation turns small faults into total outages: a ~4% node loss became a 100% platform failure because healthy nodes could not proceed without the failed ones.
Investment alone does not buy resilience: Delta had spent hundreds of millions on IT (including $150M in 2015) yet a single power-room fire still grounded the global fleet.
Legacy tiers with no graceful fallback become the recovery bottleneck: when only Deltamatic's green-screen mode survived, most agents were reduced to hand-writing boarding passes.
Systems that can never be taken offline accumulate hidden latent defects, which surface only during a genuine incident rather than a controlled maintenance window.
improvements: Design for failure as the normal case, not the exception: assume components will fail and build the platform to absorb single-component loss transparently at server, data-store, and network layers.
Establish true fault-domain isolation at the electrical transfer/control node so no single power-room event can eliminate both the primary source and the switching-in backup.
Continuously audit and validate power-cord mapping and failover paths (not just at build time) to catch single-corded/mis-mapped servers before an incident does.
Engineer graceful degradation and quorum tolerance into tightly-coupled distributed systems so partial node loss does not halt the whole platform.
Modernize or wrap legacy application tiers (e.g. Deltamatic) and ensure fallback/recovery paths are themselves resilient rather than collapsing to an unusable interface.
Create safe maintenance and test procedures for redundancy exercises (staged transfers, verified backup readiness before cutover) to prevent the test itself from causing the outage.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism: a common-mode power fault upstream of redundancy
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The trigger was a planned control action — a scheduled transfer of load onto the backup generator for testing — that precipitated a fire in the power control room. That fire failed a transformer and cut a power feed to the facility. The design intent was sound in one dimension: two utility feeds entered on opposite sides of the building to survive a localized insult such as a backhoe strike. But path diversity is not fault-domain diversity. The primary source and the switching-in backup generator both terminated at the same power-control-room equipment that burned, making the fire a common-mode failure sitting upstream of every server's dual-corded power supplies. Neither feed separation nor per-server redundancy could ride through a fault at the point where they all converged.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why a ~4% node loss became a total outage
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Only about 300 of 7,000 servers actually lacked a working alternate feed, so in raw terms roughly 4% of the fleet lost power. In a loosely-coupled system that would have been a contained, survivable event. Instead, the surviving and dual-fed servers stayed powered but could no longer communicate with the failed nodes. In a tightly-coupled distributed system, losing a subset of nodes breaks quorum, shared state, and hard dependencies, so the healthy majority cannot make forward progress. The absence of graceful degradation is what converted a partial power loss into the collapse of Delta's entire platform — check-in, baggage, fueling, scheduling, websites, kiosks, and airport displays all went dark together.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery and the legacy-tier bottleneck
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Recovery required rebooting 500 servers, and the core platform was operational again about six hours after the fire, at roughly 08:30 EST. The FAA ground stop lifted around 08:40, but the operational recovery lagged far behind the technical one: by 1:30 PM only 1,700 of ~6,000 scheduled flights were running, and cancellations continued for three days. A critical drag on recovery was the reservation stack's 52-year-old Deltamatic application; when systems returned, only its old green-screen interface worked, so most agents — untrained on it — had to check passengers in manually and hand-write boarding passes. A recovery path that was not itself designed to degrade gracefully became the constraint on getting the airline moving again.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This was not a case of underinvestment: Delta had spent hundreds of millions on IT over three years, including $150 million in 2015 alone, and CEO Ed Bastian took full public responsibility. The deeper systemic driver is that these systems can never be taken offline — not even for a short maintenance window — which is precisely why latent defects such as the 300 single-corded servers and the un-modernized legacy tier persisted undetected in production and surfaced only under a real fault. The design philosophy the incident violated is that component failure should be treated as normal and expected, to be absorbed rather than handled as an exception; the outcome showed that recovery paths themselves had not been designed to that standard.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The incident fits a durable industry pattern: electrical and power-chain infrastructure is one of the most common root causes of data-center outages, consistent with this failure originating in the power control room and switchgear rather than the IT stack. Georgia Power's confirmation that there was no grid outage and that other customers were unaffected locates the fault internally, reinforcing that the vulnerability was Delta's own power topology, not the utility. The financial magnitude — about $150 million against a Ponemon industry-average outage cost near $730,000 — shows how an airline's tight coupling of operations to a single data center can amplify a routine class of failure into a business-critical, worldwide event.

technicalDeepDive:
Mechanism, stitched from first-party statements reported in the press plus a secondary risk analysis. The initiating fault was in the electrical distribution equipment feeding Delta's Atlanta technology command center. Georgia Power's technicians 'concluded the issue was a failed switchgear' — the assembly of switches, buses, breakers and protective devices that routes incoming power and distributes it to downstream loads (the WSJ likened it to 'a fuse box at home'). Delta CEO Ed Bastian described the failing element more specifically as 'a power control module... [that] failed and caught fire.' (Whether equipment literally ignited is the CEO's characterization, not an independently documented engineering finding; a fault of this kind at a distribution bus can plausibly, but not provably from the sources, remove the utility feed and compromise the transfer path to backup generation.)

Critically, per the ASA risk note, on 8 August 2016 'Delta lost access to Georgia Powers and its reserve generator.' In a properly segregated design an automatic transfer switch would drop the utility source and pick up generator/UPS power without interrupting the protected load — that generic expectation is engineering context, not a description of Delta's specific topology, which the sources do not detail. Here the reserve was unavailable; one reported, explicitly hedged explanation (Reuters, quoted by WSWS) is that a routine test of the backup power supplies was in progress and the switchgear failure 'locked Delta out of its reserve generators.' The net effect was a genuine, un-backed loss of power to the data center.

The decisive IT-layer mechanism was partial failover. Data-center resilience assumes critical workloads either ride through on backup power or fail over to redundant systems. Delta's statement, reported by the WSJ — 'some critical systems and network equipment didn't switch over to Delta's backup systems' — with the ASA note adding Delta's 'Other systems did,' describes a non-atomic, heterogeneous failover in which a subset of critical booking and flight-operations applications and their supporting network equipment did not transfer. Because these systems are interdependent (reservations, departure control, check-in, gate/airport-departure displays), losing even a subset degraded the whole; the systems 'run everything from flight dispatching to crew scheduling, passenger check-in, airport-departure information displays, ticket sales and frequent-flier programs.' When primary power was restored the un-transferred systems did not simply resume — they required manual restart, state reconciliation and validation, which is why recovery took days rather than minutes and why cancellations cascaded well after power returned (>650 cancelled Monday, ~2,300 over three days, and an estimated ~$100 million reduction in August revenue per the ASA note citing Fortune). The WSJ ties the unreliable failover to an aging, post-merger estate ('IT systems that date from the 1990s'), consistent with a mix of platforms whose failover was neither uniform nor fully tested end-to-end. No source resolves the precise technical reason the specific systems failed to cut over; Delta said it was still 'investigating the cause.'

sourcing.confidence: Medium-high on impact, timeline, and cost (corroborated across Availability Digest and Data Center Knowledge, both re-fetched and confirmed this pass, though both ultimately trace to Delta's own estimate); medium on the physical failure mechanism, which is analytic reconstruction from secondary sources with no equipment-level RCA. No official Delta engineering post-mortem exists; primary sources (BBC article body, ECN Magazine technical piece, SEC filings) were unreachable this pass. Feed-count wording ('both feeds' vs 'one of two') is reconciled at the shared transfer node and is a terminology difference, not a contradiction in the causal chain. Note: the cited Availability Digest source gives the Ponemon average as ~$730,000 only; a previously stated '$740K / $2.4M max' range was not in the cited references and has been corrected.
